passages.title: Rudy Hartono: An Indonesian Badminton Legend
passages.text:
Rudy Hartono is one of Indonesia’s best-known badminton players. Born in Surabaya in 1949, he became famous for his achievements in men’s singles at the All England Championships, a major badminton tournament. He won the title eight times, including seven years in a row from 1968 to 1974. His eighth title came in 1976. These results made him an important name in the history of the sport.

Hartono was known for his powerful and fast playing style. At a time when badminton was becoming a source of national pride, his success attracted attention from people across Indonesia. Newspaper and magazine reports helped more fans follow international badminton, and young players had a successful Indonesian athlete to look up to. His achievements also showed that Indonesian players could compete strongly on the international stage.

Hartono’s sporting record is impressive, but a record alone does not explain why people remember an athlete. Fans may admire his determination, the pressure he handled in major matches, or the way his victories brought people together. These are interpretations of his career, rather than statistics that can be counted. What can be stated clearly is that eight All England men’s singles titles gave him a special place in the tournament’s history.

Today, Hartono is remembered as a major figure in Indonesian badminton. His career offers a useful example for students learning about sports: success can be measured through results, but the meaning of an athlete’s achievements may be understood differently by different people.

passages.title: A Mangrove Learning Center
passages.text:
A mangrove learning center stands beside a wide stretch of muddy coast. From the entrance, visitors can follow a wooden path through the trees without walking directly on the soft ground. The roots rise above the mud like tangled fingers. They help hold the soil in place and provide shelter for small animals. At high tide, water moves between the roots, bringing tiny fish and other organisms into the area.

The center has a small information room with maps, photographs, and simple displays. Local guides explain how mangroves protect coastlines and why young trees need time to grow. A viewing platform gives visitors a place to watch birds without getting too close to them. The area is not designed as an amusement park. Instead, it encourages people to observe quietly and learn how coastal habitats work.

School groups often visit in the morning, when the weather is cooler. Some students sketch the roots, while others record the animals they can see. The guides remind everyone to stay on the path, avoid littering, and leave living things where they are. These rules help protect the habitat while allowing visitors to enjoy it.

The center is useful for people who want a calm outdoor visit as well as students studying the environment. Its most important feature is the connection between direct observation and local knowledge: visitors can see the habitat and hear why it matters from people who work near it.

They help hold the soil in place

passages.title: The Day Our Class Ran a Sports Event
passages.text:
Last Friday, our class organized a small sports event for students in other classes. We planned it for two weeks. Some students prepared the schedule, while others checked the equipment and made signs for each game. I was responsible for recording the scores. I thought the job would be easy, so I did not bring an extra pen or paper.

At first, everything went well. The first basketball game started on time, and the teams followed the rules. Then, just before the next game, my pen stopped working. I looked in my bag, but I had no spare pen. The teams were ready, and the other students were waiting for me to record the results. I felt embarrassed because I had not prepared for a simple problem.

Luckily, a classmate lent me a pencil and a small notebook. I wrote down the scores carefully and checked them with the referee after each game. The event continued with only a short delay. At the end, we collected the equipment and cleaned the area together.

I was tired, but I felt proud of our class. I learned that a successful event needs teamwork and preparation. Even a small task can become difficult if we forget basic supplies. Next time, I will make a checklist before the event begins.

passages.title: My First Week as a Library Volunteer
passages.text:
When our school library asked for student volunteers, I signed up because I wanted to become more organized. During the first week, I learned that the work involved more than putting books on shelves. We had to check return dates, arrange books by category, and help students find materials for assignments.

On Monday, I placed several books about history in the science section. I did not notice the mistake until a student came looking for a biology book and found a book about ancient kingdoms instead. The librarian showed me how to read the labels and check the catalogue before moving a book. She did not get angry, but she asked me to correct the shelves and explain what I had learned.

By Wednesday, I was more careful. I checked each label twice and asked questions when I was unsure. I also noticed that some students felt shy about asking for help. I began greeting them and offering to show them where the books were. Most only needed a short direction, but a few needed help using the catalogue.

At the end of the week, I understood that being organized is not simply about keeping things neat. It also means following a system and noticing what other people need. I still made small mistakes, but I was more confident than I had been on the first day.

passages.title: The Legend of Timun Mas
passages.text:
This retelling follows a common version of the Indonesian folktale Timun Mas. An elderly couple wished for a child, and a giant named Buto Ijo promised to help them. He gave the couple a cucumber seed, but he demanded that they give him the child when she grew older. The couple accepted because they desperately wanted a family.

A golden cucumber later grew in their garden. Inside it, they found a baby girl and named her Timun Mas. They raised her with love, but as she grew, they became afraid of the promise they had made. When Buto Ijo returned to claim her, the couple told Timun Mas to run and gave her several small packets to use if she was in danger.

Timun Mas ran through fields and forests while the giant chased her. She threw the contents of the packets behind her. In many versions, the objects changed into obstacles such as thorny plants, mud, or water. Each obstacle slowed Buto Ijo, but he continued to follow her. At last, Timun Mas used the final packet, and the giant could no longer reach her. She returned safely to the couple.

The tale is often understood as a story about courage and quick thinking. Timun Mas does not defeat the giant through strength alone; she uses the help she was given and keeps moving when danger approaches. Details differ between retellings, so this passage presents one familiar version rather than a historical account.

passages.title: The Legend of Lake Toba
passages.text:
This passage retells a familiar version of the Lake Toba legend from North Sumatra. A man who lived by fishing caught an unusual fish. When he brought it home, the fish changed into a woman. They later married, but she asked him to keep her origin secret. He agreed, and they built a family together.

Years later, their son often made mistakes and sometimes behaved carelessly. One day, his father asked him to take food to the fields. The boy delayed and ate some of it on the way. When the father discovered what had happened, he became very angry and called the boy the child of a fish, breaking the promise he had made to his wife.

The woman was deeply hurt. She told her son to go to higher ground, then returned to the water. Heavy rain began to fall, and water spread across the valley. In the legend, the flooded area became Lake Toba, while the land in its middle became Samosir Island.

People tell different versions of the story, but the broken promise is central to many of them. The tale can be read as a warning about speaking in anger and failing to keep an important agreement. It also connects a landscape known today with a story passed down through generations. The legend explains cultural meaning, not the scientific formation of the lake.

passages.title: How to Prepare for Badminton Practice
passages.text:
A good badminton practice begins before you enter the court. Preparing your equipment and body helps you use the practice time well. You do not need expensive items, but you should bring the things you need and follow the coach’s safety instructions.

First, check your bag. Put your racket, a few shuttlecocks if your coach asks you to bring them, a water bottle, and a small towel inside. Wear sports clothes and shoes that are suitable for an indoor court. If your shoes are dirty or slippery, clean them before playing.

Next, arrive early enough to change and listen to the coach. Begin with a gentle warm-up, such as walking, moving your arms, and making easy steps from side to side. Do not start with your fastest movements immediately. Follow the warm-up your coach gives you, and tell the coach if you feel unwell or have pain.

After warming up, practise the drills in the planned order. Take short breaks when instructed and drink water during suitable breaks. Do not swing your racket close to another player. When practice ends, collect the shuttlecocks, check the court for rubbish, and put the equipment away.

Finally, check your bag before leaving. A simple routine helps you arrive ready, play safely, and keep the court tidy for the next group.

Next, arrive early enough to change

passages.title: How to Make a Simple Breakfast Wrap
passages.text:
A breakfast wrap is an easy meal to prepare when you need something quick before school. You can change the filling to match what you have at home. Ask an adult for help when using a hot pan or a sharp knife.

You will need one tortilla or flatbread, one cooked egg, a few slices of tomato, some lettuce, and a little grated cheese. You also need a plate, a spoon, and a pan if you want to warm the wrap. Wash your hands before handling the food. Rinse the tomato and lettuce under clean running water.

First, place the flatbread on a clean plate. Put the cooked egg in the middle, then add the tomato, lettuce, and cheese. Do not add too much filling, because the wrap may tear when you fold it. Next, fold the left and right sides toward the middle. Fold the bottom edge up and roll the wrap gently.

If you prefer a warm wrap, ask an adult to help you heat it in a pan for a short time. Turn it carefully so both sides become warm. Do not leave the pan unattended. When the wrap is ready, put it on a plate and turn off the heat.

Clean the work area and store any remaining ingredients safely. The wrap is now ready to eat. Preparing the ingredients first makes the process easier and helps you avoid rushing.

passages.title: Why Schools Should Protect Time for Physical Activity
passages.text:
Schools should protect regular time for physical activity because movement supports students’ daily routines and gives them a useful break from sitting. Academic lessons are important, but students also need opportunities to move, practise skills, and work with others. Physical activity should not be treated as wasted time.

One reason is that games and sports can teach cooperation. In a team game, students have to communicate, follow shared rules, and respond when a plan changes. These experiences can help students practise social skills in a setting different from a classroom discussion. Not every student enjoys competitive sports, so schools should offer several choices, such as walking clubs, dance, or simple movement activities.

Another reason is that a planned activity break can make the school day feel more balanced. Students who spend many hours seated may welcome a chance to stretch and change their focus. However, activity should be organized safely, with suitable equipment and alternatives for students with different abilities. Schools should not assume that one sport is right for everyone.

Some people argue that extra activity takes time away from academic subjects. This concern deserves attention, especially when lessons already feel crowded. Yet a timetable can include movement without removing essential learning. Schools can use short activity periods, active breaks, or well-planned physical education lessons.

For these reasons, schools should protect regular physical activity while keeping it inclusive and well organized. The goal is not to make every student an athlete; it is to give all students a fair chance to move, cooperate, and take part.

passages.title: Why Orangutan Habitat Protection Matters
passages.text:
Protecting orangutan habitat should be a priority because these animals depend on forests for food, shelter, and movement. When forests are broken into small, separated areas, orangutans may find it harder to reach food and safe places. Protecting individual animals is important, but it is not enough if the forest around them continues to disappear.

Forest protection can also benefit other living things. A forest is a connected system where plants, insects, birds, and mammals depend on one another in different ways. Keeping large areas healthy helps maintain places for many species, not only orangutans. Forests can also support people who rely on them, provided that resources are managed responsibly.

Some communities live near forest areas and need income from work and local businesses. Conservation plans are more likely to last when local people can take part in decisions and have realistic ways to earn a living. Simply telling people to stop using land without discussing their needs may create conflict. Protection efforts should combine clear rules, education, and practical support.

There are challenges. Monitoring large forest areas can be difficult, and conservation work requires time, funding, and cooperation. These problems do not mean that protection is impossible. They show why governments, conservation groups, businesses, and communities need to work together.

Protecting orangutan habitat is therefore not only about one species. It is also about maintaining a living environment and making careful choices about land use. Strong conservation plans recognize both ecological needs and the lives of people who share the landscape.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Orangutan habitat protection should consider forests, wildlife, and nearby communities.
Protecting one orangutan is enough to solve forest loss.
Local communities should never take part in conservation decisions.
Forest protection only matters to orangutans and no other species.
Conservation work can succeed without time, funding, or cooperation.
questions.why: The passage argues that habitat protection benefits ecosystems and requires cooperation with local communities.
questions.evidence: Protecting orangutan habitat is therefore not only about one species ... recognize both ecological needs and the lives of people who share the landscape.
wrong: Correct; it summarizes the whole passage.
The passage says protecting individuals is not enough if habitat disappears.
The passage argues that local people should take part in decisions.
The passage says forest protection can benefit many species.
The passage identifies time, funding, and cooperation as important challenges.

questions.stem: Which TWO conclusions can be drawn from the passage? Select TWO answers.
options: Conservation plans should consider the needs of people living near forests.
Protecting connected forest areas can support more than one species.
All conservation challenges can be solved immediately.
People’s income needs and wildlife protection can never be addressed together.
Monitoring forests requires no resources.
questions.why: The passage connects durable conservation with local participation and explains that healthy forests support many species.
questions.evidence: Conservation plans are more likely to last when local people can take part ... Keeping large areas healthy helps maintain places for many species.
wrong: Supported by the third paragraph.
Supported by the second paragraph.
The passage says conservation takes time and resources.
The passage argues for practical ways to address both needs.
The passage says monitoring requires time, funding, and cooperation.

rows.s: Orangutans depend on forests for food and shelter.
rows.why: This is an ecological reason to protect habitat.

rows.s: Healthy forests provide places for many species.
rows.why: This is an ecological benefit.

rows.why: This concerns community participation.

rows.s: Conservation work needs funding and cooperation.
